# Clinical Data Standards: CDISC, SDTM, and ADaM {#sec-cdisc} ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *The nice thing about standards is that you have so many to choose from.* [Andrew S. Tanenbaum]{.smallcaps}, *Computer Networks* (1981) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Sources Authored directly for this book rather than adapted from earlier course materials. Target audience: students heading to pharma or CRO statistical programming roles who have no prior exposure to CDISC. Written in response to reports from alumni that a gap in this area was felt on the first day of their industry positions. ::: ## Prerequisites Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-19. 1. What is the difference between SDTM and ADaM, and who typically specifies and builds ADaM? 2. In the CDISC convention, does `CNSR = 1` indicate a censored observation or an event? 3. What is the role of `ADSL` relative to other ADaM datasets such as `ADLB` or `ADTTE`? ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - Name the four main CDISC standards (SDTM, ADaM, CDASH, SEND) and identify which are required for FDA submissions. - Describe the data flow from CRF through SDTM to ADaM to tables, listings, and figures (TLFs). - Read an SDTM domain and an ADaM dataset and explain how rows and variables relate. - Derive a minimal `ADSL` and `ADTTE` from synthetic SDTM domains using R. - Recognize the common ADaM variable names (`USUBJID`, `PARAMCD`, `AVAL`, `CNSR`, and the population flags). - Explain the purpose of Define-XML, the annotated CRF (aCRF), and the reviewer guides (SDRG, ADRG). ## Orientation Alumni of this program who now work in pharmaceutical companies and contract research organizations (CROs) report a common experience. Their first weeks on the job bring data structures, variable names, and regulatory conventions that the statistics curriculum never covered. This chapter addresses that gap. The Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) is a non-profit that publishes data standards for clinical trials. Since December 2016, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required that sponsors submit clinical trial data in CDISC formats to support new drug applications (NDAs) and biologics license applications (BLAs). The two formats a statistician will touch are SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) and ADaM (Analysis Data Model). The organizing insight for the chapter is this: SDTM is how the data arrives at the statistician's desk, and ADaM is what the analysis team specifies, builds, documents, and analyzes. In most sponsors and CROs the work is divided. The biostatistician writes the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and, often, the ADaM specifications; statistical programmers implement the ADaM datasets and the tables against those specifications, usually with independent double programming for validation. Whichever role you take, your deliverables will, with high probability, be ADaM specifications, ADaM datasets, or the tables derived from them. ## The statistician's contribution {#sec-cdisc-human} The derivations are bookkeeping, and bookkeeping can be learned. What separates a submission that passes review from one that does not is a small number of conventions that are easy to get backwards: **Traceability is non-negotiable.** Every ADaM variable must point back to its SDTM source. The Define-XML and the ADaM specification document the mapping. Skipping the documentation does not save time; it produces an FDA submission that fails review and an ADaM that the next statistician cannot understand. **Get the censoring convention right.** The `CNSR = 1` convention is the inverse of R's `survival::Surv(event = 1)`. Converting once at the boundary (when reading ADTTE into R) with `event = CNSR == 0` is correct; converting twice or not at all silently produces wrong survival curves. Verify on every analysis. **Population flags carry inferential meaning.** The intent-to-treat (ITT) set, or full analysis set (FAS), includes every randomized patient, analyzed as randomized. A modified ITT (mITT) set excludes a small number of randomized patients by a rule the protocol states in advance (for example, no post-baseline assessment); its definition varies by sponsor and must be read, not assumed. The safety set includes every patient who received at least one dose, analyzed as treated. A per-protocol (PP) set excludes patients with important protocol deviations. The SAP pre-specifies which analysis set each analysis uses; the ADSL flags (`ITTFL`, `FASFL`, `SAFFL`, `EFFFL`, `PPROTFL`) implement the choice. An analysis set is not the estimand's population, which ICH E9(R1) defines at the level of the scientific question, but the set should be chosen to estimate that estimand. Using the wrong flag at analysis time analyzes a different group of patients than the SAP promised, and may no longer target the stated estimand. **ADaM specifications are written, then built.** The standard workflow: write the ADaM spec (spreadsheet or YAML), validate it, then implement the derivations against the spec. Building first and writing the spec from the result is a common antipattern; the spec is the contract that gets reviewed. These judgments are what distinguish defensible CDISC programming from boilerplate-following. ## The regulatory pipeline The flow of clinical trial data from collection to submission follows a standardized pipeline: 1. **Protocol** defines the trial design, endpoints, and statistical analysis plan (SAP). 2. **CRF** (Case Report Form) is the instrument sites use to record observations on each participant. 3. **SDTM** domains are built by data management from the collected CRF data and submitted to the FDA as the raw tabulations layer. 4. **ADaM** datasets are derived from SDTM by statistical programmers, against specifications the biostatistician writes or reviews. They are analysis-ready and also submitted to the FDA. 5. **TLFs** (Tables, Listings, and Figures) are produced from ADaM for the Clinical Study Report (CSR) that accompanies the submission. @fig-cdisc-pipeline shows the flow and, crucially, the row granularity at each stage, which is the quantity a statistician must track across every join. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-cdisc-pipeline %%| fig-alt: "Vertical pipeline from protocol and SAP, to the CRF %%| for site data entry, to SDTM domains such as DM, EX, AE, LB, %%| VS and DS holding one row per observation, to analysis-ready %%| ADaM datasets such as ADSL, ADTTE and ADAE, to tables, %%| listings and figures, and finally to the CSR and FDA %%| submission. Dashed annotations mark SDTM as immutable once %%| locked and ADaM as traceable back to SDTM." %%| fig-cap: "The regulatory data pipeline from protocol to FDA %%| submission. SDTM is the immutable source the statistician reads; %%| ADaM is the analysis-ready layer the statistician builds." flowchart TD P["Protocol and SAP
design, endpoints, estimands"] --> C["CRF
site data entry"] C --> S["SDTM domains
DM · EX · AE · LB · VS · DS
one row per observation"] S --> A["ADaM datasets
ADSL · ADTTE · ADAE
analysis-ready"] A --> T["TLFs
tables, listings, figures"] T --> R["CSR and FDA submission
Define-XML, aCRF, SDRG, ADRG"] S -.->|"immutable once locked"| S A -.->|"traceable to SDTM"| S ``` Two rules organize this pipeline: - **Immutability of source.** Once SDTM is locked, it is not edited to accommodate new analyses. A new analytic need produces a new ADaM variable, not a change to SDTM. - **Traceability.** Every ADaM variable must point back to its SDTM source and its derivation logic, documented in the ADaM specification and the Define-XML. ## SDTM: the FDA's view of the raw data SDTM organizes a trial's observations into **domains**, each a dataset covering one topic area. Core domains you will see include: - `DM`: demographics (one row per subject). - `EX`: exposure or dosing (one row per dose or constant-dosing interval). - `AE`: adverse events (one row per event). - `LB`: laboratory results (one row per test result). - `VS`: vital signs. - `DS`: disposition and end-of-study status. Two features of SDTM are worth noting. First, its structure is **vertical**: within a domain, each row is a single observation, and the same variable names (`USUBJID`, `VISIT`, `--TESTCD`, `--ORRES`, `--STRESN`) recur across domains. Second, dates are stored as ISO 8601 character strings such as `'2024-03-15'` or `'2024-03-15T08:30'`, not as R `Date` objects; this is an FDA submission requirement. You do not usually build SDTM as a biostatistician. You read it. ## ADaM: the analysis-ready layer ADaM datasets take SDTM as input and produce rows and columns shaped for direct use by statistical procedures. There are three principal structures: - **ADSL** (Subject-Level Analysis Dataset): exactly one row per subject. Contains treatment assignment, demographics, baseline covariates, key dates, and population flags. Every other ADaM dataset joins back to `ADSL` by `USUBJID`. - **BDS** (Basic Data Structure): one row per subject per parameter per analysis visit. Used for longitudinal, laboratory, vital-signs, and time-to-event analyses. Common examples include `ADLB`, `ADVS`, and `ADTTE`. - **OCCDS** (Occurrence Data Structure): one row per occurrence. Used for adverse events (`ADAE`) and concomitant medications (`ADCM`). A few variable-name conventions recur across every ADaM dataset you will encounter: | Variable | Meaning | |---|---| | `USUBJID` | Unique subject identifier, sponsor-wide. | | `TRT01P`, `TRT01A` | Planned and actual treatment, period 1. | | `PARAMCD`, `PARAM` | Parameter code and decoded name. | | `AVAL`, `AVALC` | Analysis value (numeric, character). | | `AVISIT`, `AVISITN` | Analysis visit (character, numeric). | | `CNSR` | Censoring indicator (0 = event; a positive integer = censored). | | `ITTFL`, `SAFFL`, `EFFFL` | Population flags. | | `ANL01FL` | Analysis record flag. | | `DTYPE` | Derivation type (e.g. `'LOCF'`). | The `CNSR` convention is the single most common source of day-one errors for new statisticians. CDISC uses `CNSR = 0` for the event and a positive integer for censoring, usually `1`, though a sponsor may use `2`, `3`, and so on to distinguish censoring reasons. The `survival::Surv()` function in R uses the opposite convention: `event = 1`. When moving between `ADTTE` and `Surv()`, convert with `CNSR == 0`, which is true for events whatever the censoring codes are. The arithmetic shortcut `1 - CNSR` works only while every censored row has `CNSR = 1`: a `CNSR = 2` becomes `-1`, which `Surv()` turns into `NA` with nothing more than a warning, and those subjects drop out of the analysis. **Controlled terminology.** CDISC publishes codelists that enumerate the valid values of categorical variables. `SEX`, for instance, takes values in `{'M', 'F', 'U', 'UNDIFFERENTIATED'}`, not `'Male'`, `'male'`, or `'1'`. Your ADaM specification will cite the relevant CDISC codelist version for each controlled variable. ::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true} ## Check your understanding: why not analyze SDTM directly? **Question.** SDTM already holds every collected value in a tidy, one-row-per-observation layout. ADaM is derived from it and adds no new data. Why build a second layer rather than fit the model on SDTM? **Answer.** Because SDTM and ADaM answer to different masters, and collapsing them costs you the thing a submission is for. SDTM is a faithful record of what was collected. It is immutable once locked, and its structure is dictated by the collection instrument rather than by any analysis. Nothing in it encodes a decision. ADaM encodes decisions, and that is the point. Which subjects are in the efficacy population. How a time-to-event value was derived and where censoring came from. Which visit counts as baseline. Those are choices made in the analysis plan, and ADaM is where they become explicit, traceable, and reviewable one at a time. Fit the model on SDTM and those decisions still get made, but inside the modeling script, mixed together, visible only to whoever reads the code. A reviewer asking 'how did you define the analysis population' would have to reconstruct it from a pipeline rather than read a flag column. The separation is the same one this book makes everywhere between raw and derived data. SDTM is `data/raw/`; ADaM is `data/derived/`. The regulatory context just makes the consequence of blurring them explicit. ::: ## Worked example: SDTM to ADaM to survival in R The example below fabricates minimal SDTM domains, derives `ADSL` and `ADTTE` for overall survival, and fits a Kaplan-Meier estimator and a Cox model. The row granularity changes at each step; tracking it is the concept. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(survival) set.seed(47) n <- 100 ``` ::: ### Fabricate SDTM domains Real SDTM has many more required variables per domain. We keep only what ADaM needs so that the pipeline is visible. The `--DTC` dates are built as ISO 8601 character strings, as SDTM stores them; conversion to `Date` happens in ADaM. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ref_start <- as.Date('2024-01-01') + sample(0:180, n, replace = TRUE) dm <- tibble( USUBJID = sprintf('STUDY01-%03d', 1:n), AGE = round(rnorm(n, 62, 10)), SEX = sample(c('M', 'F'), n, replace = TRUE), RACE = sample( c('WHITE', 'BLACK OR AFRICAN AMERICAN', 'ASIAN'), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.70, 0.20, 0.10)), ARM = sample(c('Placebo', 'Drug 50mg'), n, replace = TRUE), RFSTDTC = format(ref_start) ) ds <- dm |> mutate( hazard = if_else(ARM == 'Drug 50mg', 0.0015, 0.0030), tt_event = rexp(n(), rate = hazard), t_admin = 365 + sample(0:180, n(), replace = TRUE), obs_time = pmin(tt_event, t_admin), DSDECOD = if_else(tt_event <= t_admin, 'DEATH', 'COMPLETED'), DSSTDTC = format(as.Date(RFSTDTC) + round(obs_time)) ) |> select(USUBJID, DSDECOD, DSSTDTC) # dosing stops at a planned 52 weeks, or earlier at death ex <- dm |> left_join(ds, by = 'USUBJID') |> mutate( start = as.Date(RFSTDTC), EXSTDTC = format(start), EXENDTC = format(pmin(start + 364, as.Date(DSSTDTC))), EXTRT = ARM ) |> select(USUBJID, EXTRT, EXSTDTC, EXENDTC) stopifnot(is.character(dm$RFSTDTC), is.character(ex$EXSTDTC), is.character(ds$DSSTDTC)) ``` ::: ### Derive ADSL `ADSL` has exactly one row per subject. Every population flag, every treatment variable, and every demographic that a downstream analysis will stratify on is placed here. Here the character `--DTC` dates become `Date` values: `TRTSDT` is the first exposure start and `TRTEDT` the last exposure end, both taken from `EX`, not from the disposition date in `DS`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} exposure <- ex |> group_by(USUBJID) |> summarise(TRTSDT = min(as.Date(EXSTDTC)), TRTEDT = max(as.Date(EXENDTC)), .groups = 'drop') adsl <- dm |> left_join(exposure, by = 'USUBJID') |> mutate( TRT01P = ARM, TRT01A = ARM, AGEGR1 = cut(AGE, c(-Inf, 65, Inf), labels = c('<65', '>=65')), SAFFL = if_else(!is.na(TRTSDT), 'Y', 'N'), ITTFL = 'Y', EFFFL = SAFFL ) |> select(USUBJID, AGE, AGEGR1, SEX, RACE, TRT01P, TRT01A, TRTSDT, TRTEDT, SAFFL, ITTFL, EFFFL) stopifnot(nrow(adsl) == n_distinct(adsl$USUBJID)) ``` ::: ### Derive ADTTE `ADTTE` follows the BDS structure: one row per subject per time-to-event parameter. Here we build a single parameter, overall survival (OS). A real `ADTTE` might stack additional rows for progression-free survival (PFS), disease-free survival (DFS), or time to treatment failure (TTF). The example is a simplification in one respect worth naming. In a randomized trial, OS is usually measured from the randomization date (`RANDDT` in ADSL, derived from the randomization record in `DS`) and analyzed on the ITT set, because dosing happens after randomization and may never happen. Our fabricated subjects are all randomized and dosed on the same day, so `TRTSDT` stands in for the randomization date; on real data it should not. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} adtte <- adsl |> left_join(ds, by = 'USUBJID') |> mutate( PARAMCD = 'OS', PARAM = 'Overall Survival (days)', STARTDT = TRTSDT, ADT = as.Date(DSSTDTC), AVAL = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT), CNSR = if_else(DSDECOD == 'DEATH', 0L, 1L), EVNTDESC = if_else(CNSR == 0L, 'Death', 'Administrative censoring'), ANL01FL = 'Y' ) |> select(USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, SAFFL, EFFFL, PARAMCD, PARAM, STARTDT, ADT, AVAL, CNSR, EVNTDESC, ANL01FL) stopifnot(all(adtte$AVAL >= 0), all(adtte$CNSR %in% c(0L, 1L))) head(adtte) #> # A tibble: 6 × 14 #> USUBJID TRT01P TRT01A ITTFL SAFFL EFFFL PARAMCD PARAM STARTDT ADT #> #> 1 STUDY01-0… Place… Place… Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-01-27 2025-03-16 #> 2 STUDY01-0… Place… Place… Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-05-22 2025-07-10 #> 3 STUDY01-0… Place… Place… Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-01-01 2024-03-23 #> 4 STUDY01-0… Place… Place… Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-06-02 2024-10-21 #> 5 STUDY01-0… Drug … Drug … Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-01-13 2025-01-16 #> 6 STUDY01-0… Drug … Drug … Y Y Y OS Over… 2024-01-23 2025-04-09 #> # ℹ 4 more variables: AVAL , CNSR , EVNTDESC , ANL01FL ``` ::: ### Analyze from ADTTE Note the `CNSR == 0` conversion from the CDISC convention to `survival::Surv()`. It gives the same answer as `1L - CNSR` on this dataset, where `CNSR` is only 0 or 1, and the right answer on a sponsor's `ADTTE` that codes censoring reasons as 1, 2, and 3. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} analysis <- adtte |> filter(ITTFL == 'Y', PARAMCD == 'OS') fit <- survfit(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) print(fit) #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) #> #> n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL #> TRT01P=Drug 50mg 44 18 NA 385 NA #> TRT01P=Placebo 56 43 197 149 340 cox <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) summary(cox) #> Call: #> coxph(formula = Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) #> #> n= 100, number of events= 61 #> #> coef exp(coef) se(coef) z Pr(>|z|) #> TRT01PPlacebo 1.0676 2.9085 0.2826 3.777 0.000158 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> #> exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 #> TRT01PPlacebo 2.908 0.3438 1.671 5.061 #> #> Concordance= 0.636 (se = 0.03 ) #> Likelihood ratio test= 15.81 on 1 df, p=7e-05 #> Wald test = 14.27 on 1 df, p=2e-04 #> Score (logrank) test = 15.61 on 1 df, p=8e-05 ``` ::: The `print(fit)` output reports the median survival and event counts per arm, but the figure a reviewer expects is the Kaplan-Meier curve. We produce it with `survminer::ggsurvplot`, including the risk table that regulatory reviewers look for beneath the curve. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(survminer) ggsurvplot(fit, data = analysis, conf.int = TRUE, risk.table = TRUE, xlab = "Days from treatment start", ylab = "Overall survival probability", legend.title = "Arm", ggtheme = theme_minimal()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Kaplan-Meier overall-survival curves by treatment arm, derived from the fabricated ADTTE. The drug arm shows the longer survival that its lower simulated hazard was constructed to produce. The risk table beneath reports subjects still at risk.](19-cdisc_files/figure-html/fig-cdisc-km-1.png){#fig-cdisc-km fig-align='center' fig-alt='Kaplan-Meier plot with two descending step functions, one per treatment arm, showing the proportion surviving over time. The drug arm\'s curve stays above the placebo arm\'s throughout and the gap widens with follow-up. A risk table beneath the axis lists the number of subjects still at risk at each time point.' fig-scap='Kaplan-Meier curves derived from the fabricated ADTTE' width=100%} ::: ::: The progression of row granularity across the pipeline is the concept to retain: `dm` is one row per subject, `ex` is one row per dosing interval (one per subject here, many in a real trial, which is why `ADSL` summarizes it before joining), `ds` is one row per disposition event, `adsl` returns to one row per subject, and `adtte` is one row per subject per parameter. Tracking this at every join is how you avoid silently duplicating subjects; the `stopifnot()` calls above are the doctrinal minimum. ## The submission package A complete submission to the FDA is not only SDTM and ADaM datasets. It includes several supporting artifacts: - **Define-XML**: machine-readable metadata describing every variable in every dataset, with controlled terminology references, derivations, and provenance. Reviewers ingest it to navigate the submission. - **Annotated CRF (aCRF)**: the blank CRF with SDTM variable names annotated on each field. It is the bridge from what was collected to what was submitted. - **Study Data Reviewer's Guide (SDRG)** and **Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide (ADRG)**: narrative PDFs that explain conformance decisions, known issues, and analysis choices. - **Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP)**: pre-specifies every analysis that appears in the CSR, including populations, estimands, and sensitivity analyses. You will not usually author Define-XML by hand. Tools such as `pinnacle21` and the open-source pharmaverse packages generate it from ADaM specifications. ## The pharmaverse Until the late 2010s, most ADaM work in industry was done in SAS. Since the early 2020s (the cross-company collaboration took shape around 2022, the year `admiral` first reached CRAN), a coordinated open-source initiative called the **pharmaverse** has produced R packages that implement ADaM derivations with validation intended for regulatory use. The principal packages include: - `admiral` [@mancini2026admiral]: modular ADaM derivations. The reference implementation for `ADSL`, `ADAE`, `ADLB`, `ADTTE`, and others. - `metacore` and `metatools`: read and validate ADaM specifications. - `xportr`: export to SAS transport (XPT) format, which the FDA still requires. - `pharmaverseadam`: reference ADaM datasets for teaching and testing. At a sponsor or CRO that has adopted R, expect to encounter these packages in production pipelines. They are a more useful thing to learn than any proprietary alternative. ::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true} ## Check your understanding: the censoring inversion **Question.** You read an `ADTTE` dataset into R and fit `survival::Surv(AVAL, CNSR)` directly, without inversion. What survival curve do you produce, and how would you spot the bug? **Answer.** You produce the curve of *censoring* over time rather than the curve of survival. `Surv(time, event)` treats the second argument as 'event happened' (`event = 1`); `CNSR = 1` means 'censored', i.e. event did *not* happen. The fitted survival curve will look upside down: the treatment that delays the event will appear to have lower 'survival' because its participants accrue more administrative censoring as they live longer. The fix is `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)`. Spot the bug by sanity-checking against the median survival time or the event rate: if a treatment everyone agrees helps survival shows up worse than placebo, suspect the inversion. The error is among the most common day-one mistakes for statisticians moving from academic survival to CDISC ADTTE. ::: ## Principle in use Three habits carry a submission through review: 1. **Specs before code.** Write the ADaM specification first; implement against it. The spec is the contract; the code is the implementation. 2. **Verify the censoring convention at the boundary.** `CNSR = 0` means the event and any positive value means censored; convert once, with `CNSR == 0`, when crossing into R's `survival::Surv()`. 3. **Use population flags deliberately.** ITT, safety, efficacy, each is a substantive choice the SAP pre-specifies. Match analysis filter to spec. ## With AI assistance {.unnumbered} ::: {.callout-tip} ## Prompts to try Send a model the structure of trial data, never the data. The domains built in this chapter are fabricated and safe to paste. A real study's SDTM or ADaM holds individual patient data and the sponsor's confidential information: it goes to an LLM only through a deployment your organization has approved for that study, and often not at all. For real work, paste the variable list, the specification, or a few synthetic rows that match it (@sec-ai-governance). 1. Paste a synthetic SDTM domain, or the variable list of a real one, and ask the LLM to describe its shape, its role, and its relationship to other domains. Check whether the model correctly identifies the granularity (one row per what). 2. Give the LLM an `ADSL` specification and ask it to generate an `admiral`-style derivation. Compare its output to the `admiral` reference implementation. Does it use the correct helper functions, or does it reinvent them? 3. Ask the LLM to write a reviewer-facing explanation of the `CNSR` convention. Evaluate whether the explanation would be accepted at face value by a new statistician, or whether it contains subtle errors about which value means what. ::: ## Exercises 1. Extend the `ADTTE` in the worked example to include a second parameter, progression-free survival (PFS), stacked as additional rows. Add a synthetic progression event to the `DS` domain to support it. Verify that `nrow(adtte) == 2 * n`. 2. Build a minimal `ADAE` (OCCDS structure) from a fabricated `AE` SDTM domain. Include `AEDECOD`, `AESER`, `AESEV`, and a treatment-emergent flag `TRTEMFL` derived from whether the analysis start date `ASTDT` (from `AESTDTC`) is on or after `TRTSDT`. **Beyond this book's dependencies.** No answer key; these need packages the book does not ship, or a document you write. 3. Install `admiral` and `pharmaverseadam` from CRAN. Load `pharmaverseadam::adsl` and compare its column list to the `ADSL` built in this chapter. Which variables are missing from our simplified version, and which of them would matter for a real oncology analysis? 4. Write an ADaM specification table (in Quarto) for the `ADTTE` built above: variable name, label, type, source, and derivation. Render it to PDF. ::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true} ## Solutions to exercises 1 and 2 **1. A second parameter stacked into `ADTTE`.** BDS datasets grow downward, not sideways. A second endpoint is more rows with a different `PARAMCD`, never a second `AVAL` column, and that is the structural point the exercise is testing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(31) # a synthetic progression event, earlier than death and # only for some subjects ds_pfs <- ds |> mutate( prog_time = rexp(n(), rate = 0.0035), DSDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC), PROGDT = DSDT - round(pmin(prog_time, 200)), had_prog = PROGDT > (DSDT - 200) & DSDECOD == 'COMPLETED' ) |> select(USUBJID, PROGDT, had_prog) adtte_pfs <- adsl |> left_join(ds, by = 'USUBJID') |> left_join(ds_pfs, by = 'USUBJID') |> mutate( PARAMCD = 'PFS', PARAM = 'Progression-Free Survival (days)', STARTDT = TRTSDT, # first of progression or death; else censor at last contact DSDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC), ADT = if_else(had_prog & !is.na(PROGDT), pmin(PROGDT, DSDT), DSDT), AVAL = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT), CNSR = if_else(had_prog | DSDECOD == 'DEATH', 0L, 1L), EVNTDESC = case_when( had_prog ~ 'Progression', DSDECOD == 'DEATH' ~ 'Death', .default = 'Administrative censoring'), ANL01FL = 'Y' ) |> select(all_of(names(adtte))) adtte2 <- bind_rows(adtte, adtte_pfs) # the check the exercise asks for stopifnot(nrow(adtte2) == 2 * n) count(adtte2, PARAMCD, EVNTDESC) #> # A tibble: 5 × 3 #> PARAMCD EVNTDESC n #> #> 1 OS Administrative censoring 39 #> 2 OS Death 61 #> 3 PFS Administrative censoring 20 #> 4 PFS Death 61 #> 5 PFS Progression 19 ``` ::: `select(all_of(names(adtte)))` is what keeps the two blocks stackable. Stacking frames with different columns succeeds and fills the gaps with `NA`, which is how a BDS dataset quietly acquires columns that apply to one parameter and not the other. PFS events are at least as frequent as OS events by construction, since progression or death both count. If your version shows fewer PFS events than OS events, the composite endpoint is wrong. **2. A minimal `ADAE` with a treatment-emergent flag.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(32) # fabricated AE domain: some events precede first dose ae <- adsl |> slice_sample(n = nrow(adsl) * 2, replace = TRUE) |> select(USUBJID, TRTSDT) |> mutate( AEDECOD = sample(c('HEADACHE', 'NAUSEA', 'FATIGUE', 'NEUTROPENIA'), n(), replace = TRUE), AESER = sample(c('N', 'Y'), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1)), AESEV = sample(c('MILD', 'MODERATE', 'SEVERE'), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(.6, .3, .1)), AESTDTC = format(TRTSDT + sample(-10:200, n(), replace = TRUE)) ) |> select(USUBJID, AEDECOD, AESER, AESEV, AESTDTC) adae <- ae |> left_join(select(adsl, USUBJID, TRT01A, TRTSDT, SAFFL), by = 'USUBJID') |> mutate(ASTDT = as.Date(AESTDTC), TRTEMFL = if_else(ASTDT >= TRTSDT, 'Y', NA_character_)) |> select(USUBJID, TRT01A, SAFFL, AEDECOD, AESER, AESEV, AESTDTC, ASTDT, TRTSDT, TRTEMFL) count(adae, TRTEMFL) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #> TRTEMFL n #> #> 1 Y 191 #> 2 9 head(adae, 4) #> # A tibble: 4 × 10 #> USUBJID TRT01A SAFFL AEDECOD AESER AESEV AESTDTC ASTDT TRTSDT TRTEMFL #> #> 1 STUDY0… Drug … Y HEADAC… N MODE… 2024-0… 2024-05-23 2024-05-03 Y #> 2 STUDY0… Place… Y FATIGUE N MILD 2024-0… 2024-06-13 2024-05-15 Y #> 3 STUDY0… Place… Y HEADAC… N SEVE… 2024-1… 2024-10-08 2024-04-23 Y #> 4 STUDY0… Place… Y NAUSEA N MILD 2024-0… 2024-08-04 2024-04-18 Y ``` ::: Two conventions are worth stating, because both are easy to get wrong and neither produces an error. `TRTEMFL` is `'Y'` or `NA`, not `'Y'` or `'N'`. CDISC flag variables are permissible-value flags: absent means absent, and coding the negative case as `'N'` makes `filter(TRTEMFL == 'Y')` and `filter(TRTEMFL != 'N')` disagree on the missing rows. The comparison is `>=`, not `>`. An event starting on the day of first dose is treatment-emergent. Using `>` drops exactly the events most likely to be attributed to the drug, and the count above shows how many rows that decision moves. This flag is deliberately incomplete. A protocol's definition of treatment-emergent usually also closes the window, at `TRTEDT` plus a stated lag (often 30 days after the last dose), and counts a pre-existing event that worsens in severity after first dose. Partial `AESTDTC` dates, such as `'2024-03'`, need an imputation rule before `ASTDT` can be compared at all. The SAP states all three; the code above implements only the lower bound. ::: ## Further reading - CDISC Foundational Standards at `cdisc.org/standards/foundational`, the authoritative reference for SDTM and ADaM themselves. - [@mancini2026admiral], the `admiral` package, the CRAN implementation of the ADaM derivations. - [@fda2024conformance], the FDA Study Data Technical Conformance Guide, which states what a submission must contain. - [@ich2019e9r1], for the estimand framework that informs which analysis set, and so which population flag, an analysis should use. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-19} 1. SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) holds the regulatory view of the raw, collected clinical data, organized into domains such as `DM`, `AE`, `LB`, and `EX`. ADaM (Analysis Data Model) holds analysis-ready datasets derived from SDTM. In industry, statistical programmers typically build ADaM against specifications written or reviewed by the biostatistician, who also writes the SAP; SDTM is built by data management or clinical programmers. 2. `CNSR = 1` indicates a censored observation. `CNSR = 0` indicates the event of interest, and a sponsor may use other positive integers for other censoring reasons. This convention is the inverse of `survival::Surv()`, which uses `event = 1`, so pass `CNSR == 0` as the event. 3. `ADSL` is the subject-level anchor dataset. It contains exactly one row per subject, with treatment assignment, demographics, baseline covariates, key dates, and population flags. Every other ADaM dataset (`ADLB`, `ADTTE`, `ADAE`, and so on) joins back to `ADSL` by `USUBJID` and inherits treatment and population flags from it.
